html:
The great mosque of the town of Djenné in Mali, the largest mud-brick building in the world. The present building dates from 1906 to 1907, raised by the town's guild of masons on the site of a mosque first built in the 13th century, when Djenné's ruler is said to have converted to Islam.

The first mosque stood for centuries while Djenné grew rich on the trade of the inland Niger delta. In the 1830s Seku Amadu, ruler of the Massina state, let it fall into ruin because he thought it too grand. The new mosque was built under French colonial rule, with its famous towers and the wooden beams that stick out of the walls.

The beams also serve as scaffolding. Every year the whole town takes part in a festival to replaster the walls with fresh mud before the rains, as at the Djinguereber Mosque in Timbuktu. The mosque stands near the ancient site of Djenné-Djenno, and the old town has been a World Heritage Site since 1988.
